newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat says meeting aims to save peace with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says meeting aims to save peace with Israel.

text.p: Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said on Wednesday he hoped a meeting of U.S., European and Arab envoys would rescue Middle East peace from a crisis over Israeli settlement plans in the West Bank.

Asked why he had called the meeting for Saturday in the self-ruled Gaza Strip, Arafat told reporters in English: "To protect the peace process...and to face the breaching of (the agreement by) the Israelis."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in Russia on a trip overshadowed by growing world criticism, told a Moscow news conference he was "fed up" with charges Israel was violating peace deals with the Palestinians.
The United States, Israel's closest ally, on Tuesday tightened the noose of international pressure around the Jewish state by agreeing to send an envoy to the meeting.
"Chairman Arafat obviously feels the need to talk to friendly countries around the world, and that's appropriate," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Netanyahu, elected last year on a vow to get tough in peace talks, has enraged Palestinians by deciding to build a new Jewish settlement and to limit the first of three Israeli troop pullbacks in the West Bank to a third of what they wanted.

Palestinians accuse him of trying to circumvent them as his peace partners and of violating Israeli-PLO peace accords by planning to build the settlement on land in Arab East Jerusalem they say is due to be the subject of future negotiation.

"The conference comes at a critical time to help the peace process out of the dead-end and the international participation will help," Ahmed Abdel Rahman, general-secretary of Arafat's cabinet, told Reuters.
The U.N. General Assembly launches on Wednesday a debate expected to end in overwhelming support for a demand that Israel abandon its plans to build 6,500 houses at the site.
In a letter this week to Netanyahu, King Hussein, the Israeli leader's closest Arab peace partner, warned the lives of Arabs and Jews were sliding towards an "abyss of bloodshed".

"I'm getting, frankly, fed up with the idea that everything we do is a violation of the (peace) agreement, and everything the Palestinians say is in compliance with the agreement," Netanyahu told reporters in Moscow.

Arafat refused to take two telephone calls from Netanyahu on Monday, Israel Television has said. A PLO official said Arafat had refused more than twice since Friday to receive Netanyahu's representatives.
"We try to call him," Netanyahu said. "He doesn't want to talk. We won't force him. I think there's an attempt to create a crisis."
Israel's Ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben-Elissar, told Israel Radio: "I don't think the government has to change its decisions. We will stick to the decisions and defend them."

Netanyahu's Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani threatened again on Wednesday to close four offices in East Jerusalem that Israel says are conducting political activity in violation of peace accords.
Israel captured East Jerusalem from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East war and declared it part of its united capital while Palestinians view it as capital of a future state.

Israeli President Ezer Weizman, a peacemaker with Egypt in the 1970s whose job now is largely ceremonial, said he was actively urging both sides to salvage peace. "Don't blow it up," he said on Israel Radio. "Argue till the morning but don't blow it up."
